drafts.title: Tactile climate controls that can be operated without looking
drafts.description: Provide physical, tactile controls for temperature and fan speed so drivers can adjust cabin climate by feel while driving, avoiding the touchscreen for these primary functions.
drafts.acceptance_criterion: A driver can set cabin temperature to within ±2°F and change fan speed by at least one step within 3 seconds by touch, without looking, in 90% of evaluated trials across 20 test drivers.
assumptions: Test uses 20 representative drivers with normal vision and typical driving seating positions.
Fan speed has at least 5 discrete steps; temperature control has 1°F resolution.
Controls remain exposed and reachable while wearing gloves.
uncertainties: Exact control layout that balances reachability, aesthetics and integration with center console.
Potential conflicts with minimalistic interior designs that favor touch-only surfaces.

drafts.title: Reliable conversational voice control for common driving tasks
drafts.description: Enable voice control to understand and execute common driving commands (media, navigation, phone, climate) reliably while driving so customers can keep hands on the wheel and eyes on the road.
drafts.acceptance_criterion: System correctly recognizes and executes a defined set of 50 common drive-mode commands (examples: 'call John', 'navigate home', 'play FM 101.1', 'set temperature 70') with ≥95% accuracy in on-road noise conditions (vehicle speed up to 70 mph, typical HVAC noise) across at least 10 phone/voice profiles.
assumptions: Testing uses a standardized command set representative of typical driver requests.
On-road noise is measured per SAE J2807-like cabin noise profiles (up to ~70 dB).
Cloud-assisted recognition is allowed where connectivity is available; local fallback is acceptable when disconnected.
uncertainties: Performance across different accents and languages may vary and require larger datasets.
Privacy or regulatory constraints could limit cloud processing in some markets (see GDPR signal).

drafts.title: Consistently reliable wireless phone charging in everyday use
drafts.description: Deliver a wireless charging pad experience where phones reliably start and remain charging during normal use and short drives, minimizing interruptions and need to fumble for cables.
drafts.acceptance_criterion: For supported Qi-compatible phones, the charging pad shows an active charging state for at least 95% of insertions and sustains charging continuously for the first 30 minutes of drive time in 95% of test cases across a representative phone sample (minimum 10 popular models).
assumptions: Test phone set includes current popular phone sizes/brands sold in the target market.
Phone alignment guidance (visual or magnetic aid) is provided as part of the pad.
Pad supports common Qi charging profiles for the tested phones.
uncertainties: Extreme case phone cases, metal attachments or very large phone sizes may still cause failures.
Future phone form factors could change compatibility; ongoing validation needed.

drafts.title: Displays and HUD readable in bright sunlight with minimal glare
drafts.description: Ensure both the head-up display and the center touchscreen remain legible in bright sunlight so drivers can read speed, navigation prompts and key status indicators at a glance.
drafts.acceptance_criterion: Head-up display remains legible (driver correctly reads speed and a navigation arrow within 0.5 seconds) at ambient illumination up to 10,000 lux in 95% of trials; center display icons and critical text remain readable from the driver seating position under the same illumination with less than 10% reduction in task completion speed compared to dim-light conditions, measured across 20 drivers.
assumptions: Illumination testing uses calibrated light sources to simulate direct sunlight up to 10,000 lux.
Legibility tests use a standard set of read tasks (speed, nav cue, media title).
HUD brightness and contrast can adjust automatically with ambient sensors.
uncertainties: Extreme glare angles from aftermarket windshield treatments or unusual driver heights may degrade performance.
Trade-offs between anti-glare coatings, screen brightness, and power consumption.

drafts.title: Include heated steering wheel as part of the Cold Weather package
drafts.description: Package the heated steering wheel as a default item inside the Cold Weather (winter) package so customers who choose that package receive the heated wheel without purchasing it separately.
drafts.acceptance_criterion: The heated steering wheel is included as a standard feature in 100% of Cold Weather packages offered in the US market (no separate add-on required) for the new model year.
assumptions: Applies to US market packaging and options structure.
Statement refers to equipment bundling (inclusion), not price level.
uncertainties: Dealer-level inventory or aftermarket retrofits may still offer heated wheels separately.
Bundling decisions may vary by trim or regional marketing rules.

drafts.title: Commercial requests on pricing, financing and dealer margins (out of scope for product spec)
drafts.description: Customers request lower base price, cheaper leasing, inclusion of option packages in base price, discounts on specific packages, lower dealer margins on options, subscription pricing for heated seats, and 0% financing offers.
drafts.acceptance_criterion: This topic documents customer requests for commercial/financial changes (lower base price below USD 50,000; lease rates cheaper than competitor; include packages in base price; Comfort package -30%; 0% financing; subscription pricing for heated seats at USD 15/month). These are commercial/pricing asks and are not actionable as a vehicle product requirement.
assumptions: Pricing, leasing and dealer margin decisions are commercial and outside the technical/product scope for vehicle requirements.
uncertainties: Some packaging requests (e.g., bundling option content) are product decisions and may be handled separately from pricing negotiations.
drafts.scope_reason: Pricing, financing and dealer margin decisions are commercial matters/out of scope for vehicle product requirements.

drafts.title: Regulatory certification and privacy compliance requests (out of scope for vehicle feature requirements)
drafts.description: Customers request that the infotainment system passes Chinese CCC certification and that driver profiles satisfy GDPR data storage requirements.
drafts.acceptance_criterion: Documented customer requests for CCC certification (China) and GDPR-compliant driver profile handling are recorded; implementation of certifications/compliance is handled by legal/regulatory and software/privacy teams rather than as a product UX requirement in this draft.
assumptions: Certification and legal compliance are managed by regulatory, legal and software architecture teams and are separate from customer-facing feature specifications.
Customer expectations for privacy and certification should inform product planning but are not themselves product UI/UX acceptance criteria here.
uncertainties: Specific legal obligations and required technical changes to meet certifications can impact product timelines and capabilities.
drafts.scope_reason: Regulatory certification and legal privacy compliance are outside the scope of product feature requirements and must be handled by compliance/legal functions.

drafts.title: Requests for a specific cockpit chip (engineering spec, out of scope)
drafts.description: Customers specifically request the Snapdragon 8295 chip for the cockpit computer; this is an engineering component request rather than a customer-facing outcome.
drafts.acceptance_criterion: This request is logged: customers asked for the Snapdragon 8295 as the cockpit chip. Selection of specific chips or component part numbers is an engineering decision and therefore out of scope for customer-facing requirements.
assumptions: Chip decisions involve BOM, supplier, thermal and life-cycle considerations handled by engineering/sourcing.
If a customer-facing outcome is desired (e.g., 'system must feel responsive' or 'support specific AI features'), those should be specified instead of a chip part number.
uncertainties: Specifying a chip may conflict with supplier availability, multi-market variants, or lifecycle windows.
drafts.scope_reason: Request names a specific hardware component (engineering specification), which is out of scope for customer-facing requirements.
